paras: The threatened lynching of William Black was a reported danger in 1900 that a Black man condemned to hang at Belair (Bel Air), Harford County, Maryland, for criminal assault on a fifteen-year-old girl would be seized and lynched before his execution. At the county's request Governor Smith sent a militia company to guard the hanging, and the sheriff brought Black from Baltimore after midnight and hanged him at 7:41 a.m. on August 31, before most of the town was awake. Wire reports presented the early hanging as a lynching averted, under headlines such as "Foils Mob and Hangs His Man."

According to a Belair dispatch, Black was accused of overpowering Jessie Bradford, a fifteen-year-old girl who lived near Aberdeen, in a patch of woods on February 21, and the crew of a passing freight train said they saw the struggle. A searching party was organized, and the same dispatch said "there is no doubt the negro would have been lynched if caught then." Black instead reached Baltimore, shipped on an oyster boat and was arrested down the bay, after which he was held in the Baltimore city jail for safe keeping, tried and convicted.

While he awaited trial, another Black man, Louis Miller, was lynched at Belair for what the papers called a similar crime. Threats followed that Black "should never die a legal death," and the county authorities feared he would be "taken from them and lynched" despite his sentence.

On August 23 Judge James D. Watters of Belair called on Governor Smith on behalf of the Harford County sheriff and State's Attorney and asked for militia at the hanging, saying it was "desired to prevent any possibility of a lynching." The governor promised protection, and Sheriff Andrew Kinhart had a new scaffold built beside the Belair jail. On August 27 Black's wife went to the governor's office to plead for clemency but left without seeing him.

Reports from the last days described Black as near collapse from fear, and the sheriff said, "I am afraid that we will have trouble with him." A Belair correspondent wrote on August 30 that Black's denial of his confession had left local people "as much, if not more, incensed against him than ever," and that citizens were surprised the governor was sending Company G of the Fourth Regiment, sixty strong. Baltimore's Deutsche Correspondent reported that the company, under Capt. Andrew A. Feuss, would guard the train and the Belair jail against violence either by whites intent on lynching Black or by Black residents trying to free him.

The newspapers had announced that Black would come on a morning train and hang soon after 10 a.m., but the sheriff put him on a train that reached Belair shortly after midnight. He was hanged in the jail yard early on August 31, and the coverage reports no crowd or disturbance.

All the coverage found came from white papers, beginning with Baltimore news carried by Washington's Evening Times and the German-language Deutsche Correspondent; no Black-press report was found. Before the hanging, the Wilmington Evening Journal headlined "Military Will Guard Murderer," though Black had been convicted of assault, and the Evening Star's correspondent called the crime "a shocking one."

After the hanging a Belair wire story ran from New York to Iowa and Michigan into September, stating the assault as fact and crediting the sheriff with outwitting the threatened lynchers. Its headlines included the New York Evening World's "Foils Mob and Hangs His Man," the Louisville Courier-Journal's "Mob Violence Feared At a Maryland Gallows" and an Iowa weekly's "Hanging Averts a Lynching." A shorter Associated Press version, headed "Negro Legally Hanged" in Richmond, said the lynching was "feared even at the last moment," and a variant printed in Alexandria identified the girl as a granddaughter of Maryland's war governor.

The Belair and Baltimore dispatches dated the assault February 21, while the Wilmington and Washington Star stories of August 30 placed it "in March last." The hour of the hanging was given as 7:41 in the main wire story, 7:36 in the Alexandria Gazette and 7:15 in the Associated Press brief, and the Alexandria version named the girl Jennie rather than Jessie.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of William Black
bases: Papers reported threats that a condemned prisoner would be lynched before his legal hanging, and the governor sent militia to prevent it (A2, A5, A8); no mob act is reported.

Black died by a court-ordered hanging carried out by the sheriff under militia guard (A8, A6), not at the hands of a group acting illegally; the lynching was threatened and forestalled, not carried out (A2, A9).
Independent Baltimore, Belair and Associated Press dispatches agree that a lynching was feared, that troops were sent and that Black was legally hanged on Aug 31 (A2, A6, A7, A8, A17).

accounts.label: County authorities' request
accounts.gist: Judge Watters said the hanging might pass off quietly but the county wished to prevent any possibility of a lynching.

accounts.label: Belair correspondent
accounts.gist: Local people believed Black's original confession, were more incensed after he recanted, and were surprised that troops were sent.

accounts.label: Baltimore German press
accounts.gist: The militia would guard the train and jail against violence either by whites seeking to lynch Black or by Blacks seeking to free him.

accounts.label: Wire report after the hanging
accounts.gist: Because of threats he would never die a legal death, the sheriff brought Black in after midnight and hanged him before most of Belair was awake.

accounts.label: Associated Press short
accounts.gist: Black was hanged at 7:15; great precautions were taken against a lynching feared even at the last moment.

framing.detail: Washington's Evening Times printed the militia request and clemency plea as routine Maryland news ('Militia for a Hanging', 'Plea for Black's Life').
The Wilmington Evening Journal headlined 'Military Will Guard Murderer' though the conviction was for assault, while reporting the troops were sent to protect him.
The Evening Star's Belair dispatch called the crime 'a shocking one' and reported local anger and surprise at the troops without comment on the threats.
The post-hanging wire ran under headlines like 'Foils Mob and Hangs His Man', 'Mob Violence Feared', 'Hanging Averts a Lynching' and 'Negro Swung to Eternity', stating the assault as fact.

conflicts.note: The Belair dispatch after the hanging (A8) and the Baltimore dispatch (A2) agree on Feb 21; A12, a reprint, prints 'February 7'.
All agree it was early morning, before the announced 10 a.m.

record_check.dossier: Supported: a threatened lynching forestalled by militia guard; Black was legally hanged, not lynched.
Criminal assault on Jessie Bradford, 15, near Aberdeen (Feb 21 or March 1900); convicted.
In custody throughout (Baltimore city jail, then the sheriff); not taken.
Threats that he would never die a legal death; no mob gathering reported.
Unnamed; feared lynchers described as whites in one Baltimore paper.
0 by mob is right, but Black died by legal execution on Aug 31; the record should note the execution.
The hanging date; the threats ran from his capture to the hanging and the militia was requested Aug 23.
Corroborated by independent Baltimore, Belair and AP dispatches.
